questions.question: Explain what plastics are, distinguish thermoplastics from thermosets, and explain why plastics must be sorted by type before recycling.
questions.expected_answer: Plastics are materials made of polymers, long chain molecules formed by joining thousands of small molecules mostly derived from oil and gas; different small molecules give different polymers with different properties, such as soft polyethylene, tough heat-resistant polypropylene, stiff brittle polystyrene and clear strong PET. Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be remoulded repeatedly, so they can be recycled; thermosets such as melamine and bakelite set hard once and cannot be remelted. Plastics must be sorted because different polymers do not blend when melted together but form weak layers and lumps, so a mixed melt gives a brittle, blotchy product or cannot be moulded at all, and a single contaminant such as a PVC bottle, which degrades at PET's melting temperature, can ruin a batch; recyclers therefore pay only for clean plastic sorted by type.

questions.question: List the seven resin identification codes with the polymer each names and two common items for each, and state which have strong recycling markets in South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Code 1, PET: clear cooldrink and water bottles, some food jars. Code 2, HDPE: milk and detergent bottles, buckets and crates. Code 3, PVC: pipes and gutters, some cling film and bottles. Code 4, LDPE: shopping and bread bags, cling film and squeezable bottles. Code 5, PP: margarine and yoghurt tubs, bottle caps, straws and lunch boxes. Code 6, PS: yoghurt cups and disposable cutlery, expanded polystyrene trays and cups. Code 7, Other: polycarbonate, nylon, acrylic and multi-layer packaging such as crisp packets. In South Africa codes 1, 2 and 5 have strong markets and are widely collected and recycled; code 4 has some value if clean and dry; codes 3, 6 and 7 are rarely recycled from household waste and mostly go to landfill.

questions.question: Describe how a household bag of plastic is sorted for recycling and name four common sorting errors.
questions.expected_answer: Containers are emptied and rinsed, since food residue attracts pests and contaminates the melt, and shaken dry; caps are removed from bottles because caps are usually a different polymer, code 5, from the bottle, code 1. Each item is turned over to find its code and sorted into piles: PET bottles, HDPE bottles and tubs, PP tubs and caps, LDPE bags and film, and a separate pile of codes 3, 6, 7 and unmarked items for general waste or a specialist collector. Bottles are squashed flat to save transport space and each type is bagged separately or according to the local scheme, then taken to a buy-back centre, kerbside collection or waste picker who is paid by the kilogram. Errors: putting unrinsed containers in the bag; leaving caps on bottles; assuming every clear bottle is PET without checking for PVC; and including polystyrene trays and multi-layer crisp packets because they are plastic.
